First of all, how well does Wine work to open Windows applications? Does it have any lag attached to emulating Windows? Also, are there ever any driver errors attached to printing or working with certain files?

I've done a little bit of messing around with Ubuntu before, but now I'm considering permanently switching when I build a new PC, so does anybody know a good place to start?
I'm thinking about switching, but I have a few questions.

I don't run Wine, so I can't speak to how well it works, but I do run several Windows versions in VirtualBox at work, and it works beautifully. I get all of the niceties of Linux with just enough Windows to run the crap that demands to be run in it.
Wine results vary dramatically. Look for native replacements first. If you can't replace the application, take a look at others experience at https://appdb.winehq.org

I used to raid in WoW through wine without any lag or noticeable shenanigans, but I couldn't get Sims 2 to run... wine is typically hit or miss (it's getting better over time though.)

I would definately recommend putting ubuntu on your new machine, as well as trying out several distros like debian, elementary os, and mint.

Typically, people don't care what os they run (except here in /v/linux,) people care about the applications they can run.

With this in mind, I would recommend checking out the software market thingy in ubuntu, it's an icon that looks like a shopping bag. It has lots of free (as in beer and as in speech) software and some pay software. I just installed Veusz to plot some data for work, works like a charm and didn't cost me a dime.

To answer your question about printers, I've never had an error with a printer driver or a scanner driver. all of the driver problems that I've had have involved video cards. Cups is very stable and well tested.

To answer your final question, a good place to start is to install ubuntu on your new machine and avoid the temptation to go back when you have little problems. Find all of the applications you need to do the things that you want to do and you'll be set.

Oh, I did have issues with getting my logitech g13 to work on my gaming pc, I got it to work eventually, but it to a lot of fiddling. I was never able to get my 14 button wow mouse to work though.

What can make life easier for you is if you are somebody who uses mobile applications a lot. I say this because a lot of the most popular mobile applications have either Chrome apps that can run offline (Pocket, Sunrise, etc), or a very well functioning web app (Evernote). There also plenty of "real" apps like OpenOffice or LibreOffice for word/ppt/excel files, geary for handling multiple email accounts, and VLC handles multimedia just as well on Linux as it does on Windows. To this point, the only application that has given me trouble is Chrome remote desktop. Everything else is light years beyond where Linux was a decade back in terms of usability and compatibility. The one major warning is that if you are a big PC gamer, look at Steam's Linux library before making the jump. More and more games are supporting it, but there will always be games that are primarily for Windows.
First of all mint is WAY better than Ubuntu. Secondly, leave your old machine running Windows on, and remote in with remmina. For all but games this is a win/win.

Wine is kind of hit an miss. It's a cool piece of software but I'd try to get whatever you are trying to run to run by alternative means. I mainly just use it for evernote, I used to play battlefield 2 on Cadaga (related to WINE) and it worked well. But you'll get other stuff that just won't work.
